sample_writing: Executive summary in lieu of a word for word translation, since I'm pressed for time: Prior to filing for the current reorganization proceedings, Mt. Gox contracted for certain services from its parent company, Tibanne. The specific services are redacted in this document, but on the basis of previous reporting, I believe them to include staffing, hosting, office space, and several other clearly necessary business expenses of Mt. Gox. Tibanne has, separately, arranged with a 3rd party for provision of some of these services. That third party's name is redacted but, for your reference, I find it unlikely given the amount of space used for the redaction that the third party is Mark Karpeles, and would naively guess another Tokyo IT firm. Mt. Gox sought to sever its contractual relationship with the 3rd party, as it came to the conclusion it was unnecessary when the reconstruction process forced Gox to identify which services it consumed were not critical to operating the company. However, the contract includes the clause that even in the event of termination, Mt. Gox is obligated to continue paying the contracted fees. (Color commentary as someone who runs an IT business: this term is routinely included in contracts negotiated at arms-length. I routinely include it in my proposed MSAs, routinely have it accepted, and routinely accept the term when vendors propose it to me. It frequently makes sense in the context of the business relationship.) Tibanne, the 3rd party, and Mt. Gox have contractually agreed to a) sever the original contract, b) Tibanne pays its outstanding balances to the third party, c) Mt. Gox pays its outstanding balances to the third party on the behalf of Tibanne. Tibanne says that the amount it is invoicing represents a compromise between it and the 3rd party, with such compromise being made in times of severe economic stress for Tibanne. (pg. 3) The two invoices are for approximately $200k of Mt. Gox's approximately $7 million of liquid assets on hand. [edit to add context: I've run a small business which does software and consulting from Japan for about 8 years, and was previously a translator. I'm (notoriously among my friends) not a Bitcoin fan. If this were legal proceedings involving *my* company or required for a client, I'd spend substantially more time making sure that I understood these documents than I have here, so you get what you paid for on the above. I hold no position in Bitcoin/Gox other than being in the tech industry, though I've followed it since 2011.]

It's fairly well-known on /r/buttcoin what Purse's actual business model is, but if you're part of the peanut gallery and don't know, the magics words are "carding" and "cashing." There exists an entire ecosystem of fraud which attacks the modern economy, including the Internet ecosystem and the banking ecosystem. Part of this ecosystem is organized criminal gangs which steal credit card numbers and other identifying information -- "carders." These are, for example, Russian mobsters with tens of engineers literally on the payroll performing adversarial security research against poorly defended retailers with the goal of securing large numbers of credit cards in rich companies. (It is an unfortunate fact that there exists a nexus of this type of crime in Eastern Europe.) There exists specialization of labor in the criminal economy: just like lawyers do not pull their own teeth because they'd be bad at it and likely hurt themselves, carders do not empty credit cards. They instead generally sell dumps of multiple credit cards to "cashers", who are generally (but not always) far less sophisticated. Cashers try to turn information into actual spendable currency; this is far riskier than stealing credit cards (which leaves a digital paper trail that is extremely difficult to follow from a compromised server in the US through multiple other compromised servers, some existing in jurisdictions that are less than receptive to subpoenas). Cashers have to take a credit card and figure out how to turn it into actual money. They're quite inventive about doing this, so many of the obvious ways -- e.g. encode the credit card number into a piece of plastic then take it to an ATM in a town you don't live in and withdraw money -- are already quite locked down by the industry, which has lost a lot of money to all the easy examples. One way cashers work is to buy high-ticket items with known resale value -- say, jewelry or Macbooks. They obtain it from online merchants who routinely sell high-ticket items to first-time buyers, asking for it to be sent to an address they either control or can access. This exposes the casher to both slippage (the Macbook might be worth $3k but only net $2k when sold for cash) and to risk, because the fraudulently obtained merchandise has to touch their hands for at least one point. Savvy merchants have learned to not ship to e.g. freight forwarders, PO boxes at less-than-reputable locations, or addresses which grossly do not match the address(es) associated with the cardholder. Enter purse.io: cashing without having to touch the fraudulently obtained merchandise yourself. The casher either sign up for a new Amazon account or purchases one which has been compromised. They add the stolen credit card to the account. They then use Purse.io and buy Bitcoins by sending fraudulently obtained merchandise to the person paying Purse Bitcoins. The casher now has Bitcoins which are not in any way forensically linked to the credit card which was stolen. They turn these Bitcoins into cash by using LocalBitcoins or similar, again inserting another cutout. Purse's discount is the service fee that it and its customers earn by laundering money for criminals. There is no other reason for sufficient volume to support this business to exist.

Get an accountant. File 2017 and 2018 tax returns late. Presumably you’ll be filing as a self-employed gamer. Schedule C. Take a Net Operating Loss (NOL) carry forward against 2019. Because the business of being a gamer looks an awful lot like a hobby, you may raise some eyebrows as to whether it is a business. Consider filing Form 5213, which will give you 5 years (counting from inception) to rack up at least 3 years which are profitable. If you do, you are entitled to presumption of for-profit motive (and the NOL will likely be allowed). If you don’t, you may be asked to demonstrate whether you operated the business in a fashion clearly intending to make a profit during the 2017-2018 years. Get an accountant! Really cannot emphasize this enough.

I used to teach English to a yakuza's wife and son. He told me he was in import/export. Hah, hah, very funny in retrospect. I only found out the truth when he ran into some business rivals at my going away dinner. They took exception to somebody inviting a white guy to "their" restaurant (actually, that might not need scare quotes for all I know), and he took exception to them taking exception, and five minutes later I was surrounded by very big, very armed, very drunk, very pissed Japanese gangsters. I am probably only here to tell the tale because his wife does a very good "ALL YOU STUPID MEN ARE RUINING MY NICE EVENING!" scream, which distracted them enough for us all to get to a cab.

(Howdy Reddit, OP here.) So I think I know why you're saying that. (The theory goes something like "He is only selling his time and, if he stops working, he has nothing of value left.") You're less informed about my business than you think you are, and separately, I think that is a pretty silly distinction to make generally and a particularly silly one to make about consultancies. Why you're less than informed about my business: in addition to doing the consulting thing, I also run two software businesses and then sell a productized consultant offering. (Basically instead of having me fly to J. Random Software Company and talk to them they can buy a video of me doing it and watching it at their own pace.) In addition to these being recurring sources of revenue, they're all (heavily) dependent on the labor of people whose relationship with me is "You do stuff for me, I cut you checks." Why do I think it is a silly distinction for consultancies? Well, scroll down the article to the part about "scaling" consultancies. Do you understand that, after you get a consultancy to multiple people, the consultancy *itself* has value external to the principal? It is a thing and it can be sold. A reasonable valuation is 2x trailing year's revenues. If I were (hypothetically) interested in doing this full time, I could fairly easily hire two people, charge myself out at my current rate (not my actual rate, but for purpose of illustration, call it $20k a week) and them out at some discount to me (for illustration, $12k). Given that I'd be the rainmaker my utilization (number of weeks successfully billed per year when not e.g. prospecting clients, dealing with HR, building the business, etc) would likely be about 50% and my employees would be at 75%. Simple math says the turnover of the consultancy is about $1.4 million a year, which puts the sale value at approximately $2.8 million. Why I think it's generally silly to group a one-man consultancy with a job: you both a) get freedom to do things which employees can't, like get unlimited vacation and b) you get substantial input on the business direction in ways which can optimize for your own career goals. For example, working at my last day job, I can't tell the company "Drop what you're doing, we're giving up our moribund market segment and focusing on one which is doing better so you can pay me 10x as much." You know how hard that is to arrange when you're a solo consultant? You just stop saying "Yes" to people from the market segment you don't want to be in. Literally that simple.
